segments.say: Every study session ends with a quiet question, usually unspoken. Do I know this now? You close the book, you look at the page, and some inner gauge gives you a reading. Good, or not yet. And then, on that basis, you decide whether to carry on or to stop.

show.title: The trap of feeling like you know it

segments.say: Psychologists call this gauge metacognition, which simply means thinking about your own thinking. It's one of the most useful tools a learner has. But the research is clear that the gauge is often miscalibrated, and that it errs in a predictable direction. It tends to say, I've got this, a little before it's true.

Here is one of my favourite demonstrations. Matthew Rhodes and Alan Castel, at Colorado State University and UCLA, showed people a list of words on a screen. Some words appeared in a large font and some in a small one. For each word, participants were asked to predict how likely they were to remember it later.

show.what: Memory predictions are influenced by perceptual information

segments.say: People predicted that the large words would be remembered better. It seems natural. Big things stand out. But when the researchers tested recall, the font size made no real difference. A word in a tiny font was remembered about as well as one in a huge font. The feeling of memorability had come from how the word looked, and not from anything that would help it stick.

This is the heart of the trap. Our feeling of knowing is built from cues, and many of those cues are about how easy something feels right now, not about how well it will be remembered next week. Ease and learning are not the same thing. Sometimes they point in opposite directions.

show.title: Cues that fool the gauge
items: Having just read it a moment ago

segments.say: This also explains the rereading habit we met at the beginning. When you read a passage a second time, the words flow. You recognise the sentences before you reach the end of them. That fluency is real, and it creates a strong sense of mastery.

But the fluency is borrowed from the page, which is still in front of you. A few minutes later, when the book is closed, you may find that the knowledge doesn't come without the cue. Robert Bjork has a phrase for this: illusions of competence. You feel competent while the information is in front of you, and then the competence evaporates.

Asher Koriat and Robert Bjork made this vivid with word pairs. When a pair was shown on the study screen, with both words visible, learners judged some of them as easy and likely to be remembered. Of course they felt easy, since the answer was right there. But on the later test, learners would only be given the first word, and would have to produce the second without seeing it. For some pairs, that was far harder than learners expected, because the feeling of ease had come from seeing both words together.

show.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 2005
show.what: Illusions of competence in monitoring one's knowledge during study

segments.say: The lesson is a simple one, though not easy to follow. Judge your learning by what happens when the page is closed. If you can't produce it from memory, you can't yet count on it, no matter how familiar it looks.

show.cap: Easy to read, not always easy to recall

segments.say: None of this means you're foolish. Everyone's gauge works this way. It's built from feelings, and feelings are quick and cheap. What we need is a second source of information, one that doesn't depend on mood. And that source is a test.

There's another famous pattern that belongs here, and it's one of the most quoted findings in all of psychology. In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger at Cornell University published a paper with a memorable title: Unskilled and Unaware of It.

Students took tests of humour, logical reasoning and English grammar, and then estimated how well they had done compared with other people. The pattern was striking. The people who scored in the bottom quarter, on average, put themselves at around the sixty-second percentile. Their real score was around the twelfth.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1999
show.what: Unskilled and unaware of it: how difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments

segments.say: The researchers' explanation was neat. The skills needed to do well at a task are often the same skills needed to judge how well you've done. If you don't know the grammar rules, you also can't spot the grammar mistakes in your own work. In other words, the gap in knowledge hides itself.

It's only fair to add that this finding has been debated. Some statisticians argue that part of the pattern comes from a plain statistical effect, because when people's guesses are noisy, the lowest scorers will always seem to overestimate, and the highest will seem to underestimate. Later work suggests there is a real effect on top of that, but that it may be smaller than the popular version suggests. What holds up is the main point. Most of us are not very good at knowing what we don't know.

That last line is the useful one. Calibration can be improved, and the way to improve it is with feedback. When you're forced to compare what you thought you knew with what you could really produce, your gauge learns.

show.title: What the research agrees on
items: People are poorly calibrated about their own knowledge
Feedback and testing narrow the gap

segments.say: So how can you set your gauge straight? One of the most effective methods is surprisingly modest. It's called a delayed judgement of learning, and it was studied by Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens, and then by many others.

Learners studied word pairs. In one condition they judged whether they'd remember a pair right after studying it. In the other they waited a few minutes, and then tried to recall the answer before judging. The delayed judgements were remarkably accurate, much better than the immediate ones. The few minutes of waiting changed what the memory could tell them.

show.what: When people's judgments of learning are highly accurate predictors of subsequent recall: the delayed-JOL effect

segments.say: Why? Because when you wait and then try to recall, you're actually running a small test. The answer either comes or it doesn't, and the gauge gets real information. Immediately after study, everything is still in your mind, and every item feels solid.

In practice, you can do the same. Finish a section, and look away. Pour a cup of tea, and write down what you can recall. Then compare it with the page. The things you missed are not a failure. They're a map of where your learning is thin, and they tell you what to do next.

There's one more place where the gauge matters, and that's in deciding what to spend your time on. Nate Kornell and Janet Metcalfe studied how students allocate their study time, and the results are quite revealing.

show.title: When students choose what to study

segments.say: Participants could choose which items to study, from easy ones to very difficult ones. People tended to spend their time on the items that were already close to being learned, those at the edge of their knowledge. Metcalfe called this the region of proximal learning. It is a good strategy, in many ways: it favours items where a little effort yields the most gain.

show.what: The dynamics of learning and allocation of study time to a region of proximal learning

segments.say: But there's a catch. Ignoring the hardest items can be sensible when time is short, but it can become a habit even when time is plentiful. And if the gauge is overconfident, we put items down too early, believing we've learned them. The result is a pile of half-learned facts and a feeling of progress.
This is simple, but it isn't easy. It asks you to trust the evidence over the feeling, and to be a little sceptical of the pleasant sense of having learned something.

show.title: Setting your gauge straight
items: Wait a little before you decide
Return to items you believe you know, because you may have forgotten them by tomorrow
Keep returning to the items that failed

segments.say: There's a kind of humility in this chapter that I find comforting. Not the sort that says, I'm not good enough. It's the quieter sort that says, I might not know this yet, let's find out. It turns learning into a conversation with the facts, rather than a performance for yourself.

So, what did we learn? That our sense of knowing runs on cues like ease and font size. That fluency, from rereading, can feel like mastery. That the least skilled tend to overrate themselves, with some fair doubts about the size of the effect. And that waiting, testing and feedback tune the gauge.

Next, we turn to a method that happens to combine a lot of what we've seen. It's the old idea that the best way to learn something is to explain it, and there are some lovely experiments about what happens when you try.
